segments.caption: You scored 80 in Maths, and 70 in Science.
Which is the better result?
Maths looks better, right? Actually, it's Science!
To see why, you need a z-score.
A z-score tells you how far a value is from the mean.
Not in marks, but in standard deviations.
The formula is simple.
Take the value, and subtract the mean.
Then divide by the standard deviation.
In Maths, the class mean was 75, and the standard deviation was 10.
80 minus 75 is 5.
Divided by 10, that's 0.5.
Just half a standard deviation above the mean.
In Science, the mean was 60, and the standard deviation was 5.
70 minus 60 is 10.
Divided by 5, that's 2!
Two whole standard deviations above the mean.
Compared fairly, Science is the stronger result.
The sign tells you the side.
Positive is above the mean. Negative is below.
Zero is exactly average.
And the bigger the size, the more unusual the value.
For normal data, about 95% of z-scores fall between -2 and 2.
Beyond 3, either way, is a common outlier flag.
And in machine learning, features like age and salary are turned into z-scores, so they share one scale.
Here's the complete picture.
A z-score is the distance from the mean, in standard deviations.
The sign shows the side. The size shows how unusual.
Use it to compare different scales, and to spot outliers.
Quick quiz!
Heights have a mean of 165 centimetres, and a standard deviation of 7.
What's the z-score of someone 151 centimetres tall?
Minus 2!
151 is 14 below the mean. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and below means negative.
Follow for data science made simple!
